screens.title: Configuring a VLAN-aware Bridge
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through the canonical process for creating a VLAN-aware bridge on a KVM host. The basic claim is simple: create a VLAN sub-interface on your physical NIC, create a bridge for that VLAN, and attach the VLAN sub-interface as a bridge slave. Practically, you will use the host's network management tool to define the VLAN device, a bridge device, and a slave mapping. The example commands create a VLAN 20 device and a bridge named br20, then bring both up. After execution, verify with standard networking tools to confirm the bridge is up and the sub-interface is a member. A concrete example is a web-tier VM pool that must be isolated on VLAN 20; when configured this way, guest frames are tagged with the VLAN ID and the downstream switch treats them accordingly. A common misconception is that bridging alone isolates traffic — without VLAN tags, guests share the same broadcast domain. Also be mindful of physical switch configuration: the switch port must allow tagged traffic for the VLAN. Key verification steps include inspecting interface lists, checking bridge membership, and confirming traffic appears with the expected VLAN tag. How would you confirm a guest's traffic is correctly tagged in your environment?

keyIdea.title: VLAN Bridge Principle
keyIdea.text: VLAN sub-interfaces entrain tag information into bridged guest traffic so multiple logical networks can share a single physical NIC.

content.html:
Process Flow
Create VLAN-aware bridge
Step-by-step network commands to place VMs onto VLAN 20.
Step 1 — Define VLAN device
Create enp1s0.20 which tags outbound frames with VLAN ID 20.
Step 2 — Create bridge br20
Define bridge and set appropriate IP method for host management if needed.
Step 3 — Enslave VLAN device
Attach enp1s0.20 to br20 so guests attached to br20 carry VLAN tags.
Verification
  • Run ip a show br20 and confirm state is UP.
  • Use brctl show or ip link to check bridge members.
  • Confirm guest frames are tagged on the switch or with tcpdump.
Key Takeaway

VLAN-aware bridges let you segment traffic without extra physical NICs; always verify switch port tagging and bridge membership.

Reference command sequence
sudo nmcli connection add type vlan con-name enp1s0.20 dev enp1s0 id 20
sudo nmcli connection add type bridge con-name br20 ifname br20 ipv4.method auto ipv6.method ignore
sudo nmcli connection add type ethernet con-name enp1s0.20-slave ifname enp1s0.20 master br20
sudo nmcli connection up br20
sudo nmcli connection up enp1s0.20-slave
Concrete example
Place a pool of web VMs on br20. The host tags their traffic with VLAN 20 so the switch places them in the web-tier broadcast domain.
Common mistake
Forgetting to configure the physical switch port for 802.1Q tagging will make the VLAN invisible to hosts and guests.

screens.title: Enabling SR-IOV and Assigning Virtual Functions
screens.narratorSegment: SR-IOV is a hardware-assisted feature that presents multiple virtual functions from a single physical NIC to the host and guests. The core claim is that SR-IOV gives VMs near bare-metal network performance by bypassing the software virtual switch. To enable it, first confirm support in the system firmware and driver, then write the desired VF count into the sysfs sriov_numvfs control for the device. After creating VFs, they appear as separate PCI devices the hypervisor can assign to guests. A concrete example is enabling four VFs on a NIC so four latency-sensitive VMs each receive a dedicated VF. A frequent misconception is that SR-IOV is always the best choice; in reality it trades migration flexibility for performance because VFs are bound to physical hardware and often cannot be live-migrated. Also ensure the host kernel has the correct module and that VFs have appropriate driver bindings. Verification steps include listing the PCI devices and checking lspci output for SR-IOV support. Consider also isolating management traffic and storage traffic from SR-IOV VFs to avoid contention. How would you balance SR-IOV performance needs with cluster migration requirements?

keyIdea.title: SR-IOV Trade-off
keyIdea.text: SR-IOV offers near bare-metal I/O by exposing virtual functions, but reduces live-migration and flexibility because VFs are tied to the physical NIC.

content.html:
SR-IOV
Enable VFs and assign to guests
Hardware + kernel steps to expose virtual functions for direct guest assignment.
Prerequisites
BIOS/UEFI SR-IOV enablement, NIC driver that supports SR-IOV, and kernel access to sysfs.
Enable VFs
Write desired VF count into /sys/class/net/DEVICE/device/sriov_numvfs.
Assign VF to VM
Attach the VF's PCI address in the guest's XML for direct assignment.
Caveat
VMs using VFs often cannot be live-migrated; plan maintenance windows or fallback paths accordingly.
Example command
# Check SR-IOV support in lspci
lspci -s <PCI_BUS_ID_OF_NIC> -v | grep -i "SR-IOV"

# Enable 4 VFs on NIC enp1s0f0
echo 4 | sudo tee /sys/class/net/enp1s0f0/device/sriov_numvfs
Concrete scenario
A database VM gets a dedicated VF to reduce packet processing latency, improving predictable query response times under load.
Verification
Use lspci and ip link to see the VFs, and check guest PCI devices after assigning a VF in its XML.

screens.title: NFS vs. iSCSI for KVM Shared Storage
screens.narratorSegment: Choosing between NFS and iSCSI depends on workload requirements and operational constraints. NFS offers file-level access and is typically easier to set up: hosts mount an exported directory and VM disk images appear as files. This simplicity makes NFS a good fit for general-purpose VMs or environments where ease of management is important. iSCSI provides block-level access and behaves like a locally attached disk; it often yields better raw performance and supports advanced storage features such as multipathing. A concrete example: a lab of application servers can use NFS for convenience, while a latency-sensitive database would often perform better on iSCSI LUNs. A common misconception is that NFS cannot be used for production; the reality is that with proper tuning and dedicated storage networks, NFS performs well for many workloads. For both options, isolate storage traffic on dedicated NICs or VLANs and verify mount and access permissions. Consider also that libvirt integrates with both: define an NFS pool as a directory-based pool or an iSCSI pool that references the target IQN. Which trade-offs would you accept for your critical workloads?

keyIdea.title: Protocol Trade-offs
keyIdea.text: NFS offers ease and file-level sharing; iSCSI delivers block-level access and often superior performance for I/O-bound VMs.

content.html:
Comparison
NFS (file-level)
Simple mounts, VM images are files on the share.
  • Easy setup and central management.
  • Works well for web/app servers and test/dev pools.
  • Sensitive to network latency and file lock semantics.
Libvirt NFS pool example
sudo virsh pool-define-as nfs_pool dir --target /mnt/nfs_share
sudo virsh pool-build nfs_pool
sudo virsh pool-start nfs_pool
sudo virsh pool-autostart nfs_pool
Comparison
iSCSI (block-level)
Hosts connect to LUNs; VMs see block devices.
  • Provides low-level block access and often better throughput.
  • Supports multipathing and storage-array features.
  • Requires initiator configuration and target management.
iSCSI workflow
sudo iscsiadm -m discovery -t sendtargets -p <ISCSI_TARGET_IP>
sudo iscsiadm -m node -T <TARGET_IQN> -p <ISCSI_TARGET_IP> -l
# Define libvirt pool using the discovered LUN path

screens.title: nmcli Commands: VLAN Bridge Demo
screens.narratorSegment: In this code-first walkthrough we'll step through the nmcli sequence used to create a VLAN sub-interface and a bridge, then confirm state. The claim is practical: these exact commands can be executed on a host with NetworkManager to realize a VLAN-aware bridge. Command Demo
nmcli VLAN and bridge
Run these commands on your KVM host; verify with ip and brctl.
sudo nmcli connection add type vlan con-name enp1s0.20 dev enp1s0 id 20
sudo nmcli connection add type bridge con-name br20 ifname br20 ipv4.method auto ipv6.method ignore

screens.title: Mounting NFS and Defining a libvirt NFS Pool
screens.narratorSegment: This walkthrough covers mounting an NFS export on the KVM host and defining a libvirt storage pool that points at that mount. The claim is pragmatic: centralizing VM images on NFS enables features like live migration and simplifies image management. Start by creating a mount point, mounting the remote export, and adding an /etc/fstab entry with the _netdev option so mounts wait for networking at boot. After the share is mounted, define a directory-based libvirt pool, build it, start it, and enable autostart. A concrete example uses a mount path like /mnt/kvm_nfs_images and a pool named nfs_kvm_pool. A common mistake is incorrect export permissions or SELinux contexts preventing libvirt from writing; verify server-side export options and host mount options. Use virsh pool-list and virsh pool-info to confirm the pool is active. As you test, consider input and output characteristics: NFS latency can vary, so place high-input and output VMs on appropriately provisioned storage or isolated networks. keyIdea.text: Mount the NFS export with persistent fstab entries and use libvirt pool commands to manage VM images centrally while validating permissions and SELinux contexts.

content.html:
Storage Setup
Mount NFS and define pool
Commands to mount a share and create a libvirt pool for VM images.
sudo mkdir -p /mnt/kvm_nfs_images
sudo mount nfsserver.example.com:/exports/kvm_images /mnt/kvm_nfs_images
# Add to /etc/fstab for persistence
echo "nfsserver.example.com:/exports/kvm_images /mnt/kvm_nfs_images nfs defaults,_netdev 0 0" | sudo tee -a /etc/fstab
sudo systemctl daemon-reload
sudo mount -a
Define libvirt pool
sudo virsh pool-define-as nfs_kvm_pool dir --target /mnt/kvm_nfs_images
sudo virsh pool-build nfs_kvm_pool
sudo virsh pool-start nfs_kvm_pool
sudo virsh pool-autostart nfs_kvm_pool

# Verify
virsh pool-list --all
virsh pool-info nfs_kvm_pool
Safety Note
Confirm server-side export options and SELinux contexts so libvirtd can read and write pool files. Incorrect contexts block pool activation.

screens.title: virtio: Paravirtualized I/O for Guests
screens.narratorSegment: Virtio is a paravirtualized input and output framework that gives guests an efficient, simple A P I to interact with the hypervisor instead of emulating complex hardware. The core definition is that virtio devices present streamlined interfaces the guest kernel can implement with lightweight drivers, which reduces context switching and emulation overhead. A practical example: using virtio-net and virtio-scsi typically improves throughput for network and disk workloads relative to fully emulated devices. Another architectural point: virtio-scsi often provides advantages over virtio-blk for modern guests because it supports features like UNMAP/TRIM, better queue depth, and hot-plugging of multiple disks. A common misconception is that virtio is only a minor optimization — in many production systems it makes the difference between acceptable and excellent input and output performance. To use virtio, ensure the guest XML specifies model="virtio" for interfaces and target bus="virtio" for disks, and that the guest OS has the matching drivers. How would you verify in the guest that virtio drivers are active and being used for the main devices? virtio: Paravirtualized I/O for Guests means virtio provides a streamlined channel between guest and hypervisor that substantially reduces i/o overhead compared to emulated devices and supports modern storage features when using virtio-scsi.. In practical terms, how virtio reduces overhead and why to prefer it. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Storage Commands
virsh pool and vol
Create volumes and manage pools for guest disks.
# List pools
virsh pool-list --all

# Pool info
virsh pool-info nfs_kvm_pool

# Create a volume
virsh vol-create-as nfs_kvm_pool vm-disk1.qcow2 20G --format qcow2

# Delete a volume
virsh vol-delete /var/lib/libvirt/images/vm-disk1.qcow2
Explanation

  • vol-create-as returns the volume path which you then reference in a VM's disk source.
  • Deleting volumes requires the actual path; ensure no guests are using the volume.
Common mistake
Assuming pool-undefine removes data. Always check and explicitly delete volumes when reclaiming space.

fullNarratorScript:
Welcome. In this lesson you will explore advanced KVM networking and storage techniques that production architects regularly use. We will look at how VLAN-aware bridges let you logically segment traffic on a single physical network, and why SR-IOV can deliver near bare-metal network performance for demanding workloads. You will also learn when to choose file-level shared storage like NFS versus block-level iSCSI, and how virtio drivers reduce input and output overhead inside guests. Each topic includes concrete configuration examples and runnable command sequences so you can reproduce these setups safely. As we go, pay attention to important trade-offs: SR-IOV improves throughput but limits live migration; NFS is easy to manage but sensitive to network performance; iSCSI gives block access and often better input and output behavior. By the end you will be comfortable defining VLAN sub-interfaces, enabling VFs, creating libvirt storage pools, and verifying that guests use virtio devices. Think about a target VM that runs a high-input and output database — we will use that scenario to ground choices and show how each option affects performance, manageability, and availability.

These objectives set the learning targets for this chapter. First, you will implement advanced KVM networking configurations such as VLAN-aware bridges so that multiple isolated networks can coexist on a single physical NIC. This matters because proper segmentation improves security, traffic isolation, and traffic engineering in multi-tenant environments. Second, you will configure shared storage using NFS and iSCSI so virtual machine images can be centralized for live migration and high availability; knowing when each protocol is appropriate helps you balance simplicity and performance. Third, you will learn to use virtio drivers to obtain higher input and output throughput inside guests. Virtio reduces emulation overhead and is a prerequisite for production performance. Fourth, you will manage libvirt storage pools and volumes using virsh commands so you can script provisioning and lifecycle operations. Each objective includes the practical command sequences and verification steps you need to practice confidently and avoid common misconfigurations.

This second objectives slide emphasizes troubleshooting and design-level decisions. You will learn to troubleshoot complex networking and storage issues specific to KVM, such as mismatched VLAN tags, SELinux denial of libvirt access to NFS mounts, and storage network congestion. Next, you will practice enabling SR-IOV VFs and understand the hardware and BIOS prerequisites for direct assignment to guests; we will show how to verify VFs are created and what limitations they impose, especially around live migration. You will also develop a capacity for design trade-offs: when to pick NFS for simplicity versus iSCSI for block-level performance, and when virtio-scsi is a better fit than virtio-blk for modern guest needs. Each objective includes concrete verification steps and a short mnemonic to keep trade-offs clear. Successful completion means you can both configure and diagnose advanced setups under real-world constraints.

Let's walk through the canonical process for creating a VLAN-aware bridge on a KVM host. The basic claim is simple: create a VLAN sub-interface on your physical NIC, create a bridge for that VLAN, and attach the VLAN sub-interface as a bridge slave. Practically, you will use the host's network management tool to define the VLAN device, a bridge device, and a slave mapping. The example commands create a VLAN 20 device and a bridge named br20, then bring both up. After execution, verify with standard networking tools to confirm the bridge is up and the sub-interface is a member. A concrete example is a web-tier VM pool that must be isolated on VLAN 20; when configured this way, guest frames are tagged with the VLAN ID and the downstream switch treats them accordingly. A common misconception is that bridging alone isolates traffic — without VLAN tags, guests share the same broadcast domain. Also be mindful of physical switch configuration: the switch port must allow tagged traffic for the VLAN. Key verification steps include inspecting interface lists, checking bridge membership, and confirming traffic appears with the expected VLAN tag. How would you confirm a guest's traffic is correctly tagged in your environment?

SR-IOV is a hardware-assisted feature that presents multiple virtual functions from a single physical NIC to the host and guests. The core claim is that SR-IOV gives VMs near bare-metal network performance by bypassing the software virtual switch. To enable it, first confirm support in the system firmware and driver, then write the desired VF count into the sysfs sriov_numvfs control for the device. After creating VFs, they appear as separate PCI devices the hypervisor can assign to guests. A concrete example is enabling four VFs on a NIC so four latency-sensitive VMs each receive a dedicated VF. A frequent misconception is that SR-IOV is always the best choice; in reality it trades migration flexibility for performance because VFs are bound to physical hardware and often cannot be live-migrated. Also ensure the host kernel has the correct module and that VFs have appropriate driver bindings. Verification steps include listing the PCI devices and checking lspci output for SR-IOV support. Consider also isolating management traffic and storage traffic from SR-IOV VFs to avoid contention. How would you balance SR-IOV performance needs with cluster migration requirements?

Choosing between NFS and iSCSI depends on workload requirements and operational constraints. NFS offers file-level access and is typically easier to set up: hosts mount an exported directory and VM disk images appear as files. This simplicity makes NFS a good fit for general-purpose VMs or environments where ease of management is important. iSCSI provides block-level access and behaves like a locally attached disk; it often yields better raw performance and supports advanced storage features such as multipathing. A concrete example: a lab of application servers can use NFS for convenience, while a latency-sensitive database would often perform better on iSCSI LUNs. A common misconception is that NFS cannot be used for production; the reality is that with proper tuning and dedicated storage networks, NFS performs well for many workloads. For both options, isolate storage traffic on dedicated NICs or VLANs and verify mount and access permissions. Consider also that libvirt integrates with both: define an NFS pool as a directory-based pool or an iSCSI pool that references the target IQN. Which trade-offs would you accept for your critical workloads?

In this code-first walkthrough we'll step through the nmcli sequence used to create a VLAN sub-interface and a bridge, then confirm state. The claim is practical: these exact commands can be executed on a host with NetworkManager to realize a VLAN-aware bridge. The example defines a VLAN 20 device on enp1s0, a bridge called br20, and an ethernet slave that ties the VLAN device into the bridge. After bringing connections up, verification uses ip and brctl. A common pitfall is forgetting to bring the slave up after the bridge, which can leave the bridge with no members. Another is assuming the host will automatically tag outgoing frames; tags are applied by the VLAN device. Practically, run the commands on a maintenance host or lab, then verify with ip a show br20 and brctl show. If traffic isn't present on the VLAN, check switch port tagging and firewall rules.
